intuition:
Imagine tracing a graph with your pencil without ever lifting it off the paper — that's continuity (연속) in a nutshell: no holes, no jumps, no breaks in the path.

💡 A function is continuous at a point only when its actual value there matches the value the trend is heading toward — the definition, the limit, and the equality must all line up.

We already know a limit (극한) describes where a function is heading; continuity asks the stricter question of whether the function actually arrives there and lands exactly on that value.
definition:
A function $f$ is continuous (연속) at $x=a$ when all three conditions hold together:

$$\text{(1) } f(a) \text{ is defined} \qquad \text{(2) } \lim_{x\to a} f(x) \text{ exists} \qquad \text{(3) } \lim_{x\to a} f(x) = f(a)$$

🗣 "F of A is defined, the limit as x approaches A exists, and that limit equals F of A."

All three must hold at the same time — if even one fails, $f$ is discontinuous (불연속) at $a$. When condition (2) fails because the left-hand limit (좌극한) and right-hand limit (우극한) disagree, the break is called a jump discontinuity (도약 불연속). When conditions (1) or (3) fail but the limit itself still exists — often because just one point is missing or misplaced — the break is called a removable discontinuity (제거 가능한 불연속), since redefining that single point would fix it.

A function is continuous on an interval (구간에서 연속) when it is continuous at every point inside that interval; on a closed interval $[a,b]$ we also require the function to match its one-sided limit from inside at each endpoint.
workedExample:
Classify the discontinuities (if any) of the piecewise function below.

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 & x < 1 \\ x+3 & 1 \le x < 3 \\ 2 & x = 3 \\ x+3 & x > 3 \end{cases}$$

🗣 "F of x equals x squared for x less than one, x plus three for x between one and three, two at x equals three, and x plus three for x greater than three."

Step 1 — Check the point $x=1$. First confirm $f(1)$ is defined: using the middle piece, $f(1) = 1+3 = 4$. Now compute the two one-sided limits (편측 극한).

$$\lim_{x\to 1^-} f(x) = 1^2 = 1, \qquad \lim_{x\to 1^+} f(x) = 1+3 = 4$$

🗣 "The left-hand limit at one is one, but the right-hand limit at one is four."

Since the left-hand and right-hand limits disagree, $\lim_{x\to 1} f(x)$ does not exist, so condition (2) fails. This is a jump discontinuity (도약 불연속) at $x=1$ — the graph physically jumps from height $1$ to height $4$.

Step 2 — Check the point $x=3$. Here $f(3) = 2$ by the given piece, so condition (1) holds. Now compute both one-sided limits using the pieces on either side.

$$\lim_{x\to 3^-} f(x) = 3+3 = 6, \qquad \lim_{x\to 3^+} f(x) = 3+3 = 6$$

🗣 "Both the left-hand and right-hand limits at three equal six."

Step 3 — Compare the limit to the function value. Since both one-sided limits equal $6$, $\lim_{x\to 3} f(x) = 6$ exists, so condition (2) holds. But $f(3) = 2 \neq 6$, so condition (3) fails. Because the limit exists and only the single value $f(3)$ is "out of place," this is a removable discontinuity (제거 가능한 불연속) at $x=3$ — patching in $f(3)=6$ would make $f$ continuous there.
teachingNote: Many students stop checking as soon as they find that a limit exists, and conclude the function must be continuous there — but they skip condition (3): the limit must also equal $f(a)$, not just exist. Train students to always ask the three questions in the same fixed order — is $f(a)$ defined? does the limit exist? do they match? — and remind them that a removable discontinuity often looks perfectly smooth except for one lonely point sitting off the curve, so "the limit exists" is never the whole story.
note:
📌 A function $f$ is continuous at $x=a$ exactly when $f(a)$ is defined, $\lim_{x\to a} f(x)$ exists, and $\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = f(a)$.

$$\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = f(a)$$

🗣 "The limit of f of x as x approaches a equals f of a."

Key terms introduced: continuity/continuous (연속), discontinuity (불연속), removable discontinuity (제거 가능한 불연속), jump discontinuity (도약 불연속), one-sided limit (편측 극한), left-hand limit (좌극한), right-hand limit (우극한), and continuity on an interval (구간에서 연속).

practice.prompt: Let $f(x) = x^2 - 1$ for $x \neq 2$, with $f(2) = 5$. Which statement best describes the continuity of $f$ at $x=2$?
choices: $f$ is discontinuous at $x=2$ because $f(2)$ is undefined
$f$ is discontinuous at $x=2$ because the limit does not exist
$f$ is discontinuous at $x=2$ because the limit does not equal $f(2)$
practice.correctAnswer: $f$ is discontinuous at $x=2$ because the limit does not equal $f(2)$
practice.solution:
Step 1 — Compute the limit as $x\to 2$: $\lim_{x\to 2}(x^2-1) = 4-1 = 3$.

Step 2 — Compare to the given value: $f(2) = 5$, but the limit equals $3$, so $\lim_{x\to 2} f(x) \neq f(2)$.

Since the limit exists but doesn't match $f(2)$, condition (3) of continuity fails, making $f$ discontinuous at $x=2$ (in fact, this is a removable discontinuity, 제거 가능한 불연속).

practice.prompt:
Find the value of $k$ that makes the following function continuous at $x=3$.

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x+1 & x<3 \\ x^2+k & x \ge 3 \end{cases}$$
practice.solution:
Step 1 — For continuity at $x=3$, the left-hand limit must equal the function's value at $x=3$ (which uses the second piece, since $x \ge 3$). Compute the left-hand limit: $\lim_{x\to 3^-}(2x+1) = 2(3)+1 = 7$.

Step 2 — Compute $f(3)$ using the second piece: $f(3) = 3^2+k = 9+k$.

Step 3 — Set the two equal and solve: $9+k = 7 \Rightarrow k = -2$.

practice.prompt: Let $f(x) = \begin{cases} x-1 & x<4 \\ 10 & x=4 \\ x-1 & x>4 \end{cases}$. What type of discontinuity, if any, does $f$ have at $x=4$?
choices: $f(4)$ is undefined, so continuity cannot be checked
practice.solution:
Step 1 — Compute both one-sided limits: $\lim_{x\to 4^-}(x-1)=3$ and $\lim_{x\to 4^+}(x-1)=3$, so $\lim_{x\to 4} f(x)=3$ exists.

Step 2 — Compare to $f(4)=10$. Since $3 \neq 10$, condition (3) fails even though the limit exists — this is exactly the pattern of a removable discontinuity (제거 가능한 불연속).

quiz.prompt: Let $f(x) = x^2+1$ for $x \neq 1$, with $f(1) = 2$. Which statement best describes the continuity of $f$ at $x=1$?
choices: $f$ is discontinuous at $x=1$ because $f(1)$ is undefined
$f$ is discontinuous at $x=1$ because the limit does not exist
$f$ is discontinuous at $x=1$ because the limit does not equal $f(1)$
quiz.solution:
Step 1 — Compute the limit as $x\to 1$: $\lim_{x\to 1}(x^2+1) = 1+1 = 2$.

Step 2 — Compare to the given value: $f(1) = 2$, which matches the limit exactly.

All three continuity conditions hold — $f(1)$ is defined, the limit exists, and they're equal — so $f$ is continuous at $x=1$.

quiz.prompt:
Find the value of $k$ that makes the following function continuous at $x=2$.

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 3x-4 & x<2 \\ kx+1 & x \ge 2 \end{cases}$$
quiz.solution:
Step 1 — Compute the left-hand limit: $\lim_{x\to 2^-}(3x-4) = 3(2)-4 = 2$.

Step 2 — Compute $f(2)$ from the second piece: $f(2) = 2k+1$.

Step 3 — Set them equal: $2k+1=2 \Rightarrow k = \frac{1}{2}$.

quiz.prompt: Let $f(x) = \begin{cases} x+2 & x<0 \\ x-2 & x\ge0 \end{cases}$. What type of discontinuity, if any, does $f$ have at $x=0$?
choices: $f(0)$ is undefined, so continuity cannot be checked
quiz.solution:
Step 1 — Compute both one-sided limits: $\lim_{x\to 0^-}(x+2)=2$ and $\lim_{x\to 0^+}(x-2)=-2$.

Step 2 — Since $2 \neq -2$, the left- and right-hand limits disagree, so $\lim_{x\to 0} f(x)$ does not exist — this is a jump discontinuity (도약 불연속), not removable.
